## What did the first version of VibeFlow look like?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/vibeflow-first-version-no-ai/

**Alessia and Elia, VibeFlow (YC S25) (Ep 18):** It was VibeFlow without AI, built within a month. People could import their UIs from tools like Lovable and then "build the backend manually with this drag and drop interface" — "there was no AI involved and then it evolved afterwards."

Alessia describes a deliberately bare first version. "It was by flow without AI, so basically we allowed people to import their UIs from other tools like [Lovable] for example and then we allowed them to build the backend manually with this drag and drop interface, but there was no AI involved and then it evolved afterwards." The problem they were testing: people were combining tools like Lovable to create functional prototypes with full backends, but that meant "3 different platforms, so imagine 3 different subscriptions... it was just like a Frankenstein approach, this is how we call it." VibeFlow's answer was "an all in one solution where people could just build their backend and then export the code and have their application" and own it. They narrowed the first use case to "AI agent integration with the database," then added the AI element and launched on Product Hunt.

---

## What does Affil.ai actually do?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-does-affilai-do/

**Vivek and John, Affil.ai (YC S24) (Ep 11):** Affil.ai builds AI compliance for financial affiliate marketing. As John explains, "we help companies basically make sure that everything that they write about is meeting credit card marketing guidelines" — for example, that a creator advertises the Chase Sapphire Preferred or the Amex Gold correctly.

John lays out the problem concretely. They "help a content creator make sure that they're advertising the Chase Sapphire Preferred or the Amex Gold correctly, because... if they don't market it correctly, then the banks could be very angry at them" — banks "could take back the commissions they get from getting people to sign up for cards, or they could kick them out of the programs cause it's technically false advertising." John knew the pain point firsthand: he has "43 credit cards," tried becoming an affiliate of a credit card program "back in like 2021, 2022," and later "launched the entire affiliate program" at a travel startup, learning quirks like companies requiring you "to basically say miles instead of points" or that statement credits "have to be advertised as up to" rather than flat numbers. Coming in "with so much compliance experience" became the wedge into the space.

---

## What does Fluency mean by a "work ontology"?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-a-work-ontology/

**Finnlay Morcombe, Fluency (Ep 23):** An ontology, in Finnlay's words, is "just like a tech word for a queryable graph" of "nodes and edges" — built over time, "non-monotonic" so "the present can affect the past." Fluency's has three layers: defining what work is, knowing who's who across tools, and understanding what's being built.

"A node represents some data and an edge is the relationship." The graph "is being built over time and it's constantly changing depending on new context we get." It's "non-monotonic, which means that the the present can affect the past because sometimes you might get an email or a communication or something changes in your business which affects what we thought was the truth previously."

The three layers: the first "defines what work is"; the second makes sure "we always know it's you" since "to a computer perspective you are different in emails in Slack in the CRM"; the third understands "what is being built through these processes," "whether it's an invoice or a PowerPoint presentation or a unit of code."

---

## What does it mean to "sell before you build"?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/sell-before-you-build/

**Vivek and John, Affil.ai (YC S24) (Ep 11):** It's the YC mantra John says reworked his mind: "the best thing is just always to launch, put yourself out there, see, sell before you build, see who's actually like interested in your product before you just waste time building out a whole pitch deck trying to raise money, like building out a perfect MVP."

John calls it the number one thing YC reworked in him. The point is to launch first and see who's actually interested before wasting time on "a whole pitch deck trying to raise money" or "a perfect MVP." College, he says, taught the opposite — it tries to make you think about "what's your business model" or "what's your 7 slide deck of like your business idea," which matter when you're fundraising but not when you're truly launching a startup. The real job is to "figure out the pain point you're actually solving." If someone doesn't get into YC, John's biggest takeaway is to "really think about like selling before you build, like really take that to heart" — "it blows my mind how simple the idea is, but like it works."

---

## What does Keeyu's "wow of the week" mean?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/keeyu-wow-of-the-week/

**Jevon Le Roux, Keeyu (Ep 21):** It's a ritual Tyler, the co-founder and CEO, runs with the engineering team. Every engineer joins one 15-minute customer product call a week, hears something, then goes off to solve "a really small little thing that could actually turn out to be meaningful" — and Keeyu pushes out new features every week.

Jevon says they're "constantly pushing out new features" and customers respond really well to it. The team is split "four in Sydney, four in Pakistan," and each engineer joins one customer call for 15 minutes a week. Tracy, on calls with customers all day, messaged that she couldn't believe how excited customers were because new stuff was "coming out all the time," which keeps customers engaged.

---

## What does Nhi believe needs to change for more people in Vietnam to invest?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-vietnam-needs-for-higher-investment-adoption/

**Nhi Nguyen, MaiMoney (Ep 5):** Three game changers: financial literacy, regulation and trust, and a mindset shift. Nhi says a lot of people don't invest because they don't know where to start, that stronger regulations would bring trust in new financial products, and that the mindset has to move from short-term gains to long-term financial planning.

She calls financial literacy a key factor — a lot of people simply don't invest because they don't know where to start or how to allocate their money, so educating people about investing from a young age matters. She also points to regulation and trust: in Vietnam the fintech space is still evolving, and stronger regulations and protections would make people more confident to explore options beyond the traditional assets of real estate, bank deposits and gold. Finally, she calls for a shift in mindset — from short-term games to long-term financial planning, and from relying on family support toward more structured long-term planning for goals like retirement, a wedding, or buying a house.

---

## What does Satya miss about working at a big company?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/leaving-big-company-to-found-startup/

**Satya Tumati, Socratix AI (Ep 16):** The people — the co-workers — and the chance to work with incredible folks again, whether by hiring them or working with them in his own company. But once you start building your own company, Satya says it's hard to imagine working on someone else's dream unless it aligns so deeply that it feels like your own.

Satya worked at massive, established companies and is now building from zero. Asked what he misses, he points to the co-workers — and notes he could get a chance to work with them again if he hires incredible folks into his own company. He can't name a single thing he'd never go back to, but his bigger reflection is on ownership: "once you start building your own company it's a bit hard to imagine working on someone else's dream, unless it aligns so deeply that it feels like your own." The sense of ownership and of creating something from scratch is, in his words, so beautiful — which is why so many founders exit a company and a few years later are building something new again.

---

## What does Shakeel mean by "frameworks don't find markets"?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/frameworks-dont-find-markets/

**Shakeel Lala, Marloo (Ep 27):** The consulting reflex of building decision trees and ranked criteria to identify the "right" market sharpens thinking but doesn't surface real opportunity. 2-3 months of frameworks produced no market. 800 advisor conversations produced Marloo.

Shakeel and Hardy started "the void" — the 6–7 months between both quitting their jobs and committing to an idea — by doing what consultants do: building frameworks. Five-point lists became 20-point lists. Nothing ever ticked all the boxes. They threw the frameworks out, went back to their networks, and ran 800 customer conversations across vertical B2B SaaS markets. The conversations found the market.

---

## What does the "verbs not nouns" idea mean to Hamish McKay?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/verbs-not-nouns-hamish/

**Hamish McKay, Order Editing (Ep 15):** Hamish references an Oscar Wilde quote he loves — that "we're verbs not nouns" — meaning you should never describe yourself as, for example, "I'm a founder." Instead it's "I'm just doing the founder thing at the moment."

He applies it to his own future: for the next five years he's going to be writing, but he's not a writer — he's just writing at the moment. His post-exit dream is to spend his late 20s to 30s, hopefully financially free, doing a postgraduate masters in creative writing, tackling the scary challenge of writing a novel, and maybe making income telling stories on the internet through a YouTube channel. Part of being human, he says, is to evolve over time, and he likes never putting himself in a box.

---

## What does Y Combinator actually get you — the badge, the network, or the mentorship?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-yc-network-vs-badge/

**Alessia and Elia, VibeFlow (YC S25) (Ep 18):** Both founders pick the network. Alessia: "for me it's definitely the network... everyone wants to help each other, so that's the biggest value." Elia agrees, noting "their logo badge YC is crazy" but "the network is gonna grow with you and it's always gonna be relevant no matter the stage."

Asked which of the badge, network and mentorship matters most, both choose network. Alessia: "no for me it's definitely the network. We got the chance to meet incredible people... and they're also good people. I was really impressed by how YC managed to select very good people... everyone wants to help each other, so that's the biggest value. And the network brings you also a lot of visibility." Elia agrees but is more skeptical of the badge: "their logo badge YC is crazy, and I don't know if it's gonna change in the future... maybe it's super important early stage but maybe in the future has less important." His reasoning for the network: "the network is gonna grow with you and it's always gonna be relevant no matter the stage," because "in the batch you met amazing people that are still in contact and support you for everything," and "you can definitely always sell to [YC] startups."

---

## What early mistake did Jevon make building Keeyu?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/jevon-shopify-app-mistake/

**Jevon Le Roux, Keeyu (Ep 21):** Chasing product-led growth, Jevon built a light version of Keeyu as a Shopify app that didn't include all the integrations — on advice that the big Shopify ecosystem would make it "just explode." It didn't work: "we spent 3 4 months building it, it didn't work, we didn't get the downloads."

Some potential investors had told him the Shopify ecosystem was so big there was huge opportunity, but one person warned him "you can't expect to just put an app up on a Shopify store and then suddenly get 1 million downloads." That person was proved right. The detour gave Jevon "even deeper conviction that we sales lead," and he ties the unit economics back to "getting our ACV right."

---

## What has building Fluency cost Finnlay personally?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/personal-cost-of-building-startup/

**Finnlay Morcombe, Fluency (Ep 23):** He lists his "skateboarding ability," "mountain biking ability," and "a more extended friend network" — but says the "number one cost to be honest" is "time with family." He misses his family, his brother, his family's pets, his girlfriend, and his friends back home.

Having uprooted his life from Melbourne to SF, Finnlay says: "I miss my family. I miss my brother. I miss my family's pets. I miss my girlfriend," and his friends back home "a little bit." When he first moved he "definitely really missed my like nuclear family," but has "kind of made peace with it now," partly because "a bunch of my friends are my colleagues."

---

## What inspired Nhi to start MaiMoney?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-inspired-nhi-to-start-maimoney/

**Nhi Nguyen, MaiMoney (Ep 5):** Two things. First, her own experience navigating personal finance across Vietnam and Australia — realizing that despite studying finance, she didn't truly understand how to plan for her long-term financial future. Second, a charity group she started when she was younger, where she raised $1,500 to build a playroom at a pediatric hospital.

Nhi says MaiMoney was born out of her experiences navigating her personal finance. Growing up in Vietnam and going to Australia in her early adulthood, she found that despite working in finance she didn't truly understand how to plan for her long-term financial future, and she saw that the long-term planning she'd been exposed to in Australia was lacking in Vietnam — where the mindset around investing was very short-term or FOMO-driven. The second inspiration came from the charity group she started when she was younger: she raised $1,500 to build a playroom at a pediatric hospital, and seeing firsthand how families struggled to pay medical bills for kids struggling from cancer reinforced a belief she carries today — "financial security is more than just money. It's about giving the freedom to focus on what truly matters in life."

---

## What is "John Gpt"?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/john-gpt-doing-things-that-dont-scale/

**Vivek and John, Affil.ai (YC S24) (Ep 11):** "John Gpt" is what the founders called John manually pretending to be the AI for their first customer. There was "no actual product" — "we only built the front end" with "no actual like AI or anything." John read thousands of documents by hand at "blitz breakneck speed," and "it solved the pain point, that's all that matters."

This is their clearest do-things-that-don't-scale story. John describes it bluntly: "the AI is just us, the AI is just me." The customer would hand over thousands of documents and John would "skim read them to like absolute blitz breakneck speed," with "the AI like flagging stuff" but "barely working." They showed slides — "I'm pretty good at making decks" — and told the customer "AI worked great." John calls it "John Gpt... aka me as like the validator." The deeper point: "we would never have stumbled into this path unless we had known that somebody was going to pay for this." Only after a month of John reading "so much garbage" and the customer signing did it become "fully time to build," and they kept iterating until "the AI was basically doing all of it."

---

## What is a "world model" and why is Fluency building one?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-a-world-model/

**Finnlay Morcombe, Fluency (Ep 23):** Where an LLM "predicts the next sentence, word, what's called a token," a world model "uses the same architecture to predict the next most likely event." For Fluency it represents "how work gets done in a business" — graph-based — so you "put work map in and it'll predict what's going to happen next. Work map out."

Finnlay distinguishes it from large language models: a world model "uses the same architecture to predict the next most likely event," and "it's not representing text. It'll represent something like a video game or represent a manufacturing floor." For Fluency, "it represents how work gets done in a business. So, it's graph based."

The payoff he describes: "effective super agents on top of your process" that can run workflows "fully autonomously," and the ability to "put in like what a future state looks like" and predict "how is it going to affect the team? How's it going to affect your revenue?" He believes the best way to do this is "a sovereign world model per customer," and notes one investor "heads up AI at Princeton" and is "super focused on building out world models." Timeline: "1.5 8 to 12 weeks," act two "9 months."

---

## What is a wallet led marketing platform?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-wallet-led-marketing-platform/

**Brian Pham, Litecard (Ep 8):** Brian Pham describes Litecard as a "wallet led marketing platform and wallet, meaning Apple and Google Wallet" — the wallets people use every day for bank cards and boarding passes, repurposed as a media channel for brands and retailers.

Brian's pitch starts from a marketing problem: it's tough for a brand or retailer to reach an end customer. SMS reads as spam and many countries don't send SMS for marketing, email "doesn't go into your inbox anymore. It goes into your social, you know, promotions, inbox," and channels like YouTube, Google and Facebook are "becoming more expensive by design." His conclusion: "As a brand and a retailer, you would definitely have a problem in the next 10 or 20 years around where to spend your media to acquire and retain a customer." Litecard's answer is to use Apple and Google Wallet — which people already use for bank cards and boarding passes — as that new media channel.

---

## What is AIducation, Hung Bui's learning platform?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-ai-education-hung-bui/

**Hung Bui, AIducation (Ep 10):** Introduced as Vietnam's first AI powered learning platform, built by Vietnamese for Vietnamese. Hung describes it as an all in one personalized platform that takes the student as the core and builds tools around them for parents, teachers and schools too.

Hung says you can call it AI education or you can call it education: a platform that supports personalized education. It knows everything about a child — their tendency for learning, their strengths, which areas they are underperforming in — and more specifically how to get the student to become better in areas that matter like mathematics and English. It's an all in one platform with a wide variety of tools designed for parents, schools and teachers as well, because, in Hung's words, the journey of education is not something that the children or the students undergo all by themselves — they go with the parents, they go with the teachers, they go with the school.

## What is Butter?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-butter-sam-richardson/

**Sam Richardson, Butter (Ep 13):** Butter is the app to hang out with new friends. It helps young adults find and build friendships by connecting over social plans — think weeknight dinners, going for a run, grabbing a coffee — and its tagline is "invent yourself."

Sam, Butter's founder, frames it as more than a friendship app — a lifestyle companion where you can create the life you want and become the person you want through connection. It's built around frequency and proximity of connection by meeting over the things you already love doing. It's not just a platform for people experiencing disconnection; it's also for people with a niche interest they love and want to share. Butter has already hit 10,000 users and is gearing up to launch across Australia.

## What is co-founder matching like at EF and YC?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-cofounder-matching-is-like/

**Alessia and Elia, VibeFlow (YC S25) (Ep 18):** Elia calls it "one of the most important process in a startup." At EF in Paris "they celebrate break up" so you don't lose time — he met around 60 people in three days. The YC co-founder matching platform is described as "like a dating platform... like a tinder or Bumble."

Elia joined EF, Entrepreneur First, in Paris last year — "a program like to do co founder matching." The mechanic: "you try to match with people... and after you have to see if you match or not on the topic on the professional side on the personal side." What stood out: "there it's super funny because they celebrate break up so it means that when you break... you don't lose time, you need to figure this out super fast." He was "trying very hard, like I met I think like 60 people in like three days," but couldn't find anyone "in the same mentality as me which is like super hardcore mentality, like I want to work seven days of the week." On the YC co-founder matching platform "they were all amazing people," but "it's like a dating platform, it's like a tinder or Bumble" where you need both a personal connection and to know how the person actually works.

## What is Dime?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-dime/

**Abby Huang, Dime (Ep 1):** Dime is a marketing platform founded by Abby Huang that connects brands and Gen Z consumers through a network of student ambassadors, data-driven campaigns, and in-person events. It has worked with brands like ByteDance and Casetify.

Dime works with a range of clients — from large companies that have IPO'd or do billion-plus revenue down to smaller startups that had great products and traction. Abby doesn't gate clients on hitting a certain revenue mark; she also takes a lot of sales and client calls advising smaller companies that may be interested in Dime's solution down the line.

---

## What is Fluency?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-fluency/

**Finnlay Morcombe, Fluency (Ep 23):** Fluency is "a platform that maps how work actually happens in Fortune 500 organizations." It gets deployed onto everyone's laptop, takes screenshots, scrapes system and network logs, and builds a "work ontology" — a queryable graph of how work gets done.

Finnlay introduces himself as "one of the co-founders of Fluency." The platform is "deployed onto let's say everybody's laptop inside of an organization" and "we see everything that happens. We take screenshots. We scrape like system logs." From all of it Fluency builds what he calls a "work ontology" — "a queryable graph" of "nodes and edges" that is "non-monotonic, which means that the the present can affect the past."

There are three use cases today. First, businesses "don't actually know what their processes are how they get done," and Fluency captures and gives them that information. Second, "once we've found all of your workflows, processes, and tasks, we tell you how to improve them. Usually that's through automation." Third, "measuring the ROI on change itself" — all "in aggregate" because "we don't allow individual employee monitoring or productivity indexing."

---

## What is gymii.ai and what problem does it solve?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-gymii/

**Selina Li, gymii.ai (Ep 2):** gymii is "an AI powered consumer app, that has the goal of making nutrition tracking easy and social." Instead of manually logging food, you take a photo or snap a video of a meal and the AI breaks it down into dishes, ingredients, calories, macronutrients and micronutrients.

Selina built gymii to solve two problems at once. First, manual nutrition tracking is a chore — so gymii lets users "just simply take a photo or snap a video of the meal" and the AI does the breakdown, "making the process super, super seamless." Second, tracking used to be "such an isolating experience," so gymii adds a social, shareable layer: users can share their meals, see what friends are eating, like and comment, get inspiration and share their journey. When users onboard, gymii captures their goals so that every meal's nutritional information is shown as aligned to those goals.

---

## What is Hamish McKay's most controversial startup hot take?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/founder-hot-take/

**Hamish McKay, Order Editing (Ep 15):** "Fuck growing to be as big as possible" — for certain people. Hamish's point is that different types of people want different types of businesses, and people should build businesses that they want to operate and want to be in.

He thinks it's actually quite sad and unfortunate that there isn't more of a community or public thesis by founders that you can be intentional about how you grow your business and predefine the parameters of what would give your life the most joy. Some people just want to make yogurt, some want to make alcohol, some want to grow a business and sell it in a few years — all super fair paths. But the media glamorizes huge-valuation, gigantic companies and billion dollar aspiration, when going down that path is very stressful, takes basically your entire 20s and potentially your 30s, and isn't even guaranteed.

---

## What is Keeyu and what problem does it solve?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-keeyu/

**Jevon Le Roux, Keeyu (Ep 21):** Keeyu is "an AI powered platform for proactive post purchase ecom ops." When a shopper hits buy, there's angst that the order won't arrive on time as promised — and normally "the brand doesn't know something's gone wrong until the customer says where is my order." Keeyu fixes that ops issue proactively, before the customer even asks.

Jevon describes Keeyu as the only solution that tracks an order "from the moment it's placed, paid for, processed, picked, packed, shipped, delivered and returned in real time," watching countless metrics to see whether it isn't going to reach the customer on time as promised, then taking proactive action. Where everyone else is trying to manage complaints faster, Keeyu's framing is: what if there were no complaints at all. As Jevon puts it, help desks "manage complaints, q prevents them" — Keeyu fixes the root cause that causes a complaint so they never happen.

---

## What is Known and what does Celeste Amadon mean by "intelligence for human connection"?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-known-celeste-amadon/

**Celeste Amadon, Known (Ep 25):** Known is a dating product Celeste co-founded with Asher; she introduces herself as "the co founder and CEO of known, where we're building intelligence for human connection." Instead of swiping, Known does deep onboarding and finds you one compatible person at a time.

Celeste describes a product designed to remove the parts of dating apps people dislike most — which she lists as "swiping," "chatting," "being ghosted," and "having too many options or too few." Known's pitch is "a lot less volume but more precision": it will "find you one person and hopefully you like them," and because the onboarding is so in-depth, "maybe there's only 10 people in the entire city" who are compatible with you.

Scarcity is deliberate. If you say no, "we might not find you another person for a week, it could be two weeks," and Known "can't guarantee" when it will find another match because "there's not an endless supply of people that are just right for you." Celeste contrasts this with competitors where you can "essentially swipe via chat," which "still creates the same market dynamics" and "choice paradox."

---

## What is MaiMoney and what problem does it solve?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-maimoney/

**Nhi Nguyen, MaiMoney (Ep 5):** MaiMoney is a fintech platform in Vietnam that gives everyday investors access to wholesale investment products and the technology to grow their wealth. Nhi's framing: "we want to bridge the gap by making investing more simple, as simple as savings" while providing significantly higher returns.

Nhi, the CEO, says traditional savings accounts in Vietnam offer a lower return but high security, while investment products are either too complex or not accessible for the everyday Vietnamese investor. MaiMoney bridges that gap by making investing as simple as savings and providing significantly higher returns to help retail investors build their wealth. It does this by partnering with licensed fund managers who manage the investments, while MaiMoney provides the tech and infrastructure — handling onboarding, customer servicing, and even sales and marketing for the fund manager products. At the time of the conversation the platform had reached $2 million in investments and was growing 45% month over month.

## What is Order Editing?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-order-editing/

**Hamish McKay, Order Editing (Ep 15):** Order Editing is a software company that online shoppers use to make changes to their order after they buy something online, while online retailers pay a monthly subscription to use the software. Hamish McKay describes it as giving customers a "Grace period" to make changes — just like you can do on Amazon — but brought to Shopify specifically.

The way it works is mostly their own technology, their own IP, that guarantees the retailer's system doesn't get the order until Order Editing says so. Some systems they've integrated with or worked through API calls, but the majority of the time they've built the IP themselves. Hamish calls it "very simple but very effective."

## What is Paire?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-pair-sock-brand/

**Nathan Yun, Paire (Ep 26):** Paire is a sustainable apparel brand co-founded by Nathan Yun that "uses material science to create clothes that are comfortable, functional and sustainable." It started with socks and is now "more of an underwear company because we sell 60% underwear."

Nathan's one-line mission statement is that "pair uses material science to create clothes that are comfortable, functional and sustainable." He started it with his best friend Rex, who is a specialist in materials and textiles, out of a passion for sustainable fashion and a desire to "fight fast fashion with better ethical and sustainable products, so that if people want to buy the product they would already be doing good for the planet." They began with socks to prove the model with one very simple product, then two years later launched underwear and t-shirts — and underwear in particular "has done super well," now making up 60% of sales.

## What is Phonely and what problem does it solve?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-phonely/

**Will Bodewes, Phonely (YC S24) (Ep 28):** Phonely lets you "answer your phone with AI that talks exactly like a person." If you have a receptionist or use a call center, Will says Phonely can automate "about 80 or 90%" of those workflows and save you "about 70%" of what you'd be paying.

Will describes Phonely in two sentences: "we allow you to answer your phone with AI that talks exactly like a person. So if you have a receptionist or use a call center, we can automate right now about 80 or 90% of those workflows using artificial intelligence and save you about 70% of what you would be paying." What it does best is reliability of voice agents at scale — when you have 10, 15, 20, 30,000 calls a day "and you want to make sure that every single call gets handled perfectly."

## What is Reforge Labs, Robert's new startup?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-reforge-labs/

**Robert Huynh, Nook / Reforge (Ep 7):** After Nook, Robert took another swing with a new co-founder, Oscar, building Reforge Labs — which builds performance marketing agents: an AI data analyst that sifts through performance and marketing data to do creative insights, creative research, and data crunching of reports.

Robert says he decided to "have another swing at the whole startup game" because he loves taking on big challenges, and found a new co-founder, Oscar. "What Reforge Labs does is we build performance marketing agents." He explains that behind all the advertising you see on TikTok there's a marketer who doesn't enjoy the data-heavy part of their job — so Reforge built "a AI data analyst that can go and sift through all that performance and marketing data" to handle creative insights, creative research, and data crunching of the reports.

## What is Sam's long-term vision for Butter?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/butter-long-term-vision/

**Sam Richardson, Butter (Ep 13):** Sam wants to create a world where every in-person interaction is built on Butter — so that no matter where you went or what you did, you could always find the community you wanted. He believes that unlock would change how people live: they'd move cities more, take that job, try that new thing, meet that new person, knowing they'd always have a foundation of community and friends.

He wants Butter to be the lifestyle destination for anyone at any point in their life to build community and "invent yourself," powering the "offline internet." He sees it as a timely topic amid AI, the post-COVID shift in how people connect, and Gen Z actively rejecting the doom scroll and seeking pre-digital experiences.

## What is Sisterwould and what makes it different?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-sisterwood/

**Floriye Elmazi, Sisterwould (Ep 9):** Sisterwould is a premium hair care brand, scientifically formulated with skincare ingredients for your hair and scalp, and an inclusive beauty brand whose products carry Braille and a tactile imprinting system for the blind and visually impaired community.

Floriye's founding insight was that "we should be treating our hair the same way we do the skin on our face" — detoxing, exfoliating and removing build up, with multi-purpose products that combine scalp care and hair care. On top of the formula, Sisterwould added Braille and its own tactile system of lines for shampoo and dots for conditioner, plus a sensory layer of texture, scent and tone so blind and visually impaired people can differentiate the products further. Floriye sums up the mission this way: "everyone deserves to be seen and included."

## What is StrongRoom's next big move?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/knowing-which-markets-not-to-enter/

**Joe Zhou, StrongRoom AI (Ep 17):** Joe says the next big move is to make no moves at all. He believes it's more important to know which market you're not going to enter than which one you are — so you'll see StrongRoom pull out of a bunch of markets that aren't relevant and focus on substance abuse and addiction.

"The funny thing is the next big move is to make no moves at all." Joe's reasoning: "sometimes it's more important to know which market you're not going to enter rather than which market you're going to enter." StrongRoom is at a place where it needs to know which market not to enter, so "you'll see the big moves is us pulling out of a bunch of markets that's not relevant and focusing on substance abuse and addiction." Areas like rewards, aged care and adherence — where StrongRoom had very little market share and spent too many resources building things that didn't matter — are exactly the distractions he's removing to stabilise the core, which has a near-monopoly in several analytics areas in Australia.

## What is the best advice Brian Pham ever received?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/best-advice-never-go-to-sleep-curious/

**Brian Pham, Litecard (Ep 8):** "Never go to sleep curious." Brian got it from an Apple executive he'd built a relationship with over 6 to 12 months of email and LinkedIn — advice he asked for from someone with "decades in the industry," expecting something about data or science.

Brian says he spoke to an executive from Apple "maybe like a year ago" who "helped us build inside the Apple ecosystem, introduce us to the right people and the culture." When they finally got on a call after months on email and LinkedIn, Brian asked what advice he'd give startups "from all your decades in the industry," expecting "anything around like data and science." Instead the executive "just told me one thing he said, never go to sleep curious." Brian says it stuck because his own first idea for Litecard came to him "when I was nodding off, going to sleep, and I was like, this is a really good idea. I'm going to write it down."

## What is the best place to start a business in 2025?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/best-place-to-start-a-business-2025/

**Brian Pham, Litecard (Ep 8):** Brian's answer is Silicon Valley. Asked for the best place to start a business in 2025, he said "Australia was a close second to be honest," but "it seems like Silicon Valley is the closest you are to America is the generally... the fastest is what I've seen."

Asked where he'd start a business in 2025 "if I was to do it all again," Brian named Silicon Valley as the fastest path, with Australia "a close second to be honest." His reasoning is speed: "the closest you are to America is the generally, like you said, is the fastest is what I've seen." It echoes his broader view that Australia is a strong testing ground but the US offers the fastest route to scale.

## What is the half-sentence pitch test?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/half-sentence-pitch-test/

**Shakeel Lala, Marloo (Ep 27):** If your proposition is sharp enough, someone will want to buy before you've finished describing the product. Shakeel hit this around the tail of the 800-conversation period.

The test forces you to compress until only the irreducible value remains. If you need three sentences, the proposition isn't tight yet.

---

## What is the most misunderstood thing about what Joe did?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/the-most-misunderstood-thing-joe/

**Joe Zhou, StrongRoom AI (Ep 17):** That he bought it to flip it. Joe says a lot of people — especially private equity people and investors — assumed he'd turn around and flip it in 18 months. But that "has not even once crossed my mind"; he bought StrongRoom to tackle substance abuse and addiction.

Joe says the misunderstanding is that "a lot of people think I'd buy it to flip it," and "that has not even once crossed my mind until so many people start mentioning it." Some private equity people and some investors assumed "I'll just turn around and flip it in 18 months." But founding and investing for a flip "doesn't really drive me." He bought StrongRoom "because I want to tackle substance abuse and addiction," and "the mission of strongroom now is to make the world a safer place" — what they're building will be saving lots of lives every day. As he says in the rapid fire: when he does something he's all in — "Strongroom dies, I'm going down with the ship right now, I'm not backing out."

---

## What is the most valuable lesson Floriye learned as a founder?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/sisterwood-most-valuable-lesson/

**Floriye Elmazi, Sisterwould (Ep 9):** That she wishes she'd known about founder stories, podcasts, communities and mentoring before she started — instead of just learning along the way. She and Rina got mentoring, joined communities, did courses and networked, and even reached out to bigger beauty brands; one was Tara from mermaid hair, who, even though she was a competitor, still gave them advice.

Floriye's takeaway is "don't be afraid to reach out, ask questions" and join other women doing the same thing. She believes that if she'd had that support before starting, it would have helped her get where she wanted to be a lot quicker and make fewer mistakes — and now she can help others back by sharing her own journey.

---

## What is the most valuable lesson Hung Bui learned as a founder?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/hung-bui-most-valuable-lesson/

**Hung Bui, AIducation (Ep 10):** That each of us has a different version of reality, and he was so immersed in his own that he never got a reality check on whether others would want his product. "It took me a year to fix that mistake."

Hung says he was so immersed in his own view of reality and what would be a good product that he "did not really have a reality check on whether or not others would also want my product." His takeaway is to put the product in front of people early: "don't be ashamed of the product that you're building, just show them even if it's like really bad right now, but at least you all know if that's something that they would want and use."

---

## What is Umami Papi?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-is-umami-papi/

**Ethan Yong, Umami Papi (Ep 20):** Umami Papi is Australia's cult chili oil brand, founded by Ethan Yong. The name is a play on words — umami is a Japanese word for flavour and Papi is a Spanish word for father figure, so put together it means "flavour daddy."

The brand started off with just chili oil and now has a couple more products, with one more on the way. Ethan's ethos is that if it tastes good and there's a lot of flavour in it, he'll make it spicy or not spicy — but currently there's an element of chilli in all the products.

---

## What makes Phonely different from other voice AI companies?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/how-phonely-is-different/

**Will Bodewes, Phonely (YC S24) (Ep 28):** Will names three things: "two and a half years of battle scars of just obsessing over one problem," a PhD background that lets them build, train and optimize their own models, and being opinionated so customers don't have to prompt engineer or pick a model — "it just is gonna work out of the box."

Will says most competitors tell you to "plug your own model in" — start with a blank canvas and figure it out yourself. Phonely is opinionated instead: "this is how voice agents should behave," solving the downstream problems so customers don't have to prompt engineer. "You don't need to know the model, you don't need to know the infrastructure, you don't need to adjust the VAT parameters." His design principle: "how do we make things as simple as possible but no simpler." They started researching this about two and a half to three years ago, "back before voice AI was even a term."

---

## What should I think about before moving abroad to a new country?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/how-to-move-abroad-as-founder/

**Stephen Turban, Lumiere Education (Ep 22):** Stephen treats it as "a two way door" — usually reversible, so trust your intuition early (you can sense your trajectory in a city within a few months). His strongest practical advice: throw parties and create things yourself rather than waiting to be invited in.

Stephen moved to Vietnam in his early 20s after deferring a McKinsey start date to its farthest option, giving him a 4-5 month window to do something new; he came to learn Vietnamese (he already spoke Chinese) and "just loved it." His advice to someone considering the same: it's "a two way door," usually reversible, so just go. "You should trust your intuition early on" — having moved to five or six cities, four outside the US, he found that within about four months you can sense whether a place is an easy or hard fit. And the practical one: "one thing you should consider is throwing parties." He rarely gets invited to parties but throws a lot of them — "if you are the one proactively creating something, especially when you're new, be the one to create stuff, don't wait for other people to invite you in."

---

## What surprised Andy Miller most about Heaps Normal's customers?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/heaps-normal-best-selling-beer/

**Andy Miller, Heaps Normal (Ep 19):** They were really blown away to learn that Heaps Normal was the best selling beer — out of all beers, inclusive of alcoholic and non alcoholic — at some of their favourite bars in Sydney and Melbourne a couple of years ago. It was a real signal this wasn't just a passing trend.

They were really blown away to learn that Heaps Normal was the best selling beer out of all beers at some of their favourite bars in Sydney and Melbourne a couple of years ago — and this is inclusive of alcoholic and non alcoholic. That blew them away and was a real signal that this wasn't just a passing trend.

Andy also points to seeing Heaps Normal show up in interesting cultural media spaces — cultural commentators, comedians and musicians, and channels like the Potato Advocate referencing it in their content. That says they're doing what they set out to do, which was to influence culture. He notes that drinking culture in Australia has changed dramatically in the last five years: where five years ago it was weird not to drink, now it's weird to ask someone why they're not drinking.

## What traction has Known seen so far?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/known-traction-numbers/

**Celeste Amadon, Known (Ep 25):** Celeste won't share live numbers, but says in Known's beta — "back in the late summer and early fall of 2025" — they set up "around 1,500 dates" and "know of a couple hundred couples that are dating." Known has since launched in San Francisco, which is "going better than our beta did."

Celeste says "we don't share those numbers publicly," but in beta Known set up "around 1,500 dates" and knows of "a couple hundred couples that are dating currently" — traction she dates to "the late summer and early fall of 2025." Known "just launched in San Francisco," and while she is "not sharing numbers from that yet," she says it's "going better than our beta did" on user acquisition, with dates "hopefully" launching "next week."

Looking ahead, she says "I hope that we have a million users and we set up a million couples" within the next year, and is "excited to see people outside of San Francisco using it because it's already working in SF."

## What was Celeste Amadon's Marina Green fundraising moment?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/marina-green-moment-celeste/

**Celeste Amadon, Known (Ep 25):** While "walking along the Marina Green with a potential investor" during her raise, a woman grabbed Celeste by the wrist and said "you don't know me but I know you because you set me up with my boyfriend" — after being "single in San Francisco for seven years." The investor's reaction: "you paying them?"

Celeste says someone first stopped her to say "oh my God I see you all over TikTok," and then, about 10 minutes later, a woman grabbed her wrist with the line about being set up with her boyfriend after seven years single in San Francisco. Celeste was "bewildered but obviously very excited" — she says "anytime I find out that people are dating from known it makes my day."

The investor, walking off, asked "you paying them?" Celeste said no, "but that's a great idea." Her takeaway: "when you're creating a positive impact on people's life, they want to say thank you."

---

## What was Hung Bui's first startup before AIducation?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/hung-bui-first-startup-personal-ai/

**Hung Bui, AIducation (Ep 10):** It was called Personal AI and it focused on the mental side — a service that let you talk to AI pals or friends, similar to character AI at the time, aimed at a new generation who prefer to talk to their idols like anime characters.

Hung says Personal AI did have users, but he realized it could be much more than that. When he looked at the data, "most of the stress actually came from education," so he concluded that a full fledged platform taking care of not just the mental side but also the education side "would be the perfect solution." That insight is what turned Personal AI into AIducation — though he's candid that they failed for quite some time before they finally found out what they should be building.

## What was it like cooking for Gordon Ramsay?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/cooking-for-gordon-ramsay/

**Ethan Yong, Umami Papi (Ep 20):** Ethan was a contestant on Gordon Ramsay's Food Star. He calls it one of the most real experiences for him — being in the kitchen, cooking for Gordon Ramsay, and having him critique his food. Ramsay said his product "was absolutely delicious," which Ethan describes as a very gratifying and fulfilling moment he'll never forget.

## What was Robert's biggest regret with Nook?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/robert-biggest-regret-nook/

**Robert Huynh, Nook / Reforge (Ep 7):** Not pivoting sooner. Robert looks back fondly on the impact Nook made and the team he upskilled, but says "My biggest regret was probably not pivoting sooner."

Robert names the cause of the downfall as the number of hidden costs and profitability issues — and the deeper problem that he "never thought that we'd work in a field that I had no expertise in, in a market I had no expertise in, in a language that I'm like only semi comfortable speaking and working in a professional setting in." Despite that, he looks back fondly because Nook brought lots of jobs and upskilled a team he's still proud of. His regret is the timing: "My biggest regret was probably not pivoting sooner."

---

## What was the Brisbane conference moment for Marloo?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/brisbane-conference-moment-shakeel/

**Shakeel Lala, Marloo (Ep 27):** A week before the Financial Advice Association of Australia conference at the end of 2024, Shakeel and Hardy vibe-coded a working Marloo demo. They paid for an exhibitor stand. Financial advisors tried to buy it on the spot — before the product was real.

By that point Shakeel could describe Marloo in a single sentence and watch advisors physically relax. The half-sentence pitch test: if your proposition is sharp enough, someone will want to buy before you've finished describing the product. The vibe-coded demo at FAAA in Brisbane was the public confirmation.

---

## What was the funniest robot failure during training?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/robot-training-failures/

**Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics (Ep 14):** At a real restaurant you get a stack of napkins to fold one by one. Early on the robot would pull out many napkins from the stack at once, making a big mess on the table when it was only supposed to fold one. Later, once the model got really good, another failure was pulling the napkin too fast so it slipped off the table.

Jason recounts that at a real restaurant they'll give you a stack of napkins which you have to fold one by one. The robot initially would make the mistake of pulling out many napkins from the stack, "and then now you have a whole big mess on the table where tons of napkins are at the center of the table" when you're only supposed to fold one. They trained the robot to handle those scenarios — whenever it grabbed multiple napkins it would put the extra ones back onto the stack, though that created a messy stack on the side it then had to deal with. His broader point: real-world physical AI, or embodied AI, is actually very complex — if you handle one scenario well, there might be other scenarios you didn't expect. As the model got really good, another failure case was that it pulled the napkin too fast so the napkin just slipped off the table. Besides those scenarios, the robot was "pretty much like 100% in folding a napkin that's present in front of it."

---

## What was the hardest day Nam remembers as a founder?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/hardest-day-as-founder/

**Nam Nguyen, TruthSystems (YC S25) (Ep 24):** Fundraising the pre-seed in January in Poland — cold, getting "a lot of nose back to back," and up against a deadline from his parents that he'd have to go back to school if nothing happened. Nam says as a founder "you sign up to get punched in the gut every single day."

Nam says he could answer simply by saying every day is hard. The one that stands out: when they first began fundraising their pre-seed, "it was like January in Poland." It was cold, fundraising outside San Francisco "is just not ideal," and they were "getting a lot of nose back to back." He was close to a deadline — his parents had said that if nothing happened by then, he'd have to go back to school. To get through it he relied on three abstractions he gave himself: whether the work aligned with his core values, the fact that he genuinely enjoys solving hard problems, and that he got to solve them with his co-founder, someone he really enjoyed working with.

---

## What was the moment Floriye thought the business might break?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/sisterwood-oh-no-moment/

**Floriye Elmazi, Sisterwould (Ep 9):** It was the Covid pandemic combined with the bottles collapsing. There was "so much fear in starting a business," and as the bottles were failing Floriye asked herself "am I meant to start this." Her way through was treating it as solving a problem and finding a solution to get past that stage.

Floriye says "the starting journey is always the hardest," and persisting through that is a big hurdle for a lot of founders. The contrast came later: she messaged Rina to say they were getting organic sales with no ads running, people purchasing and repurchasing, and felt they'd hit a milestone — proof of how far they'd come from the moment she wasn't sure she was meant to start at all.

## What was their most rewarding moment building the company?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/bene-pennsylvania-factory-moment/

**Kiki and Elan, Sourmilk (Ep 4):** On the way to a Christmas gathering in Pennsylvania, Elan stopped at a huge co-manufacturer for a factory tour. After she left, two young women who run the social accounts of competing yogurt brands recognized her from Kiki's social media, called her back, and told the owner they needed to support Sourmilk — proof that competitors were rooting for them.

The story took place in December, about one month into Kiki being on social media. Kiki had gone home to California; Elan was in New York and "heading out to Pennsylvania to go to a family gathering," so she stopped at "one of the biggest... co manufacturers" — a facility doing "tens of thousands of units of yogurt a week," far beyond what Sourmilk could currently accommodate. Elan did the whole factory tour, "got along with them," and was "selling hard on why they should care about [Sourmilk]." After she pulled out of the parking lot she got a call from a random number — someone at the factory asking her to turn around because the owner wanted to meet her. When she went back, "there are two other young women who are like our age who work for one of the competitors," and they "immediately recognized Elan from [Kiki's] social media" and told the owners "we need to work with them... we need to support them." The takeaway for the founders: "there's just been this like very strong camaraderie between other yogurt companies wanting to help us... because a rising tide lifts all boats."

---

## What were the biggest challenges building MaiMoney?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/maimoney-biggest-challenges/

**Nhi Nguyen, MaiMoney (Ep 5):** Nhi names three: building trust in the fintech and financial services space in Vietnam, bridging the gap between traditional finance and technology, and scaling. She says products like managed funds were designed for institutional or high-net-worth investors, and adapting that for the everyday investor while keeping the process seamless was a big learning curve.

The first challenge was building trust — being a newer startup in fintech and financial services in Vietnam, where people are naturally cautious. The second was bridging the gap between traditional finance and technology: many investment products, especially managed funds, were designed for institutional or high-net-worth investors, and adapting that concept for the everyday investor while keeping the process seamless was a big learning curve for Nhi and her team, including making the platform integrate smoothly with the fund managers' infrastructure. The third is scaling — she says MaiMoney has been fortunate to have early traction, but growing the user base and getting people more comfortable with investing is an ongoing effort, which is why they double down on product simplicity and making every touchpoint frictionless.

---

## What would Brian Pham do differently if he started Litecard again?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/what-brian-would-do-differently/

**Brian Pham, Litecard (Ep 8):** Study the data faster. Brian says "if I was to do it all over again, I would decide and study the data faster" — instead of getting excited about the technology first and figuring out the data later, he'd ask how big and how global the problem is from day one.

Brian admits that "as most founders do," he gets "excited about the technology and try and figure out the data after." If he did it again, "I would bring that back as early as possible" and ask "in terms of money dollar value, where am I solving a problem? How big is the problem? Can it be bigger and is a global problem or not?" He believes that "if I just ask myself those questions at the very beginning of the journey, may be able to speed it up 2 or 3 times." Even so, he frames it as a fine line "between being an optimist and a realist," and that "everything that we learned along the way shaped our business as we are today."

---

## What would Floriye text her day-one self in one sentence?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/advice-to-day-one-founder-self/

**Floriye Elmazi, Sisterwould (Ep 9):** She would tell her day-one self: "I'm really proud of you and don't be scared and keep going." Floriye says she's now in a place she would never have dreamed of when she started three or four years ago.

The reason it lands so hard is her starting point: she became a single mom with no finances, didn't know how she'd take care of her boys, and felt she had no choice but to start a business. She didn't want to get old one day and feel she "never tried and never did what I was passionate about." For Floriye, it's "not just about creating this brand of Sisterwould" — the name itself means being there for others "just like a sister would be."

---

## What's it like to build a medium sized company on purpose?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/building-medium-sized-company/

**Hamish McKay, Order Editing (Ep 15):** Both Hamish and his co-founder Carol decided before they started the business that they were going to grow what could only be described as a medium sized company — there was no ambition to build a massive organization. A lot of how they think about scaling is driven by speed and medium-term ambitions rather than longer-term ones.

This is why Order Editing currently exists as an add-on via Shopify only and has decided not to expand to other e-commerce platforms. Hamish admits you could sell to a brand like Nike for hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, and that building for the long term would require diversifying onto other platforms. But that would take two or three years to build, get to market and grow awareness — whereas spending those two to three years investing in Shopify could get them to 10 or 12 million ARR. It's nonsensical, he says, when you're not looking to be the operator of your business in five years time.

---

## What's next for MaiMoney in 2025?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/maimoney-2025-roadmap/

**Nhi Nguyen, MaiMoney (Ep 5):** Nhi says 2025 is about scaling the platform: introducing goal-based investing features for life goals like a wedding, buying a house, or retirement; working with more fund managers to originate more products; and exploring how to integrate AI to make investing more personalized.

She notes MaiMoney launched almost one year ago — on the 29th of March — and the plan for 2025 is to scale. That means goal-based investing features so people can set goals and get customized portfolios for each one, expanding the network of fund managers to deliver more financial products, and exploring ways to integrate AI for more personalized recommendations. Her vision: to make investing as effortless as possible, so people can set their goals and MaiMoney provides the technology to help everyday investors get there.

## What's next for Umami Papi?

URL: https://foundersinmotion.tech/questions/umami-papi-next-product/

**Ethan Yong, Umami Papi (Ep 20):** A hot honey. Ethan describes it as a spicy honey made from Australian honey — "salted caramel meets sweet chilli." By the time the episode airs it's likely already at Coles, or at least online.
